question: Which of the following is NOT associated with the Chalukyas?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shore Temple at Mamallapuram.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram was built by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), so it is not a Chalukya monument; the other three are linked with the Chalukyas (शोर टेम्पल — पल्लव कृति, चालुक्य नहीं)

 

• The Aihole Inscription was written by Ravikirti for Pulakesin II and celebrates Chalukya victories.

 

• The Pattadakal group of temples was built by Chalukya kings and queens, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

 

• The Vesara style, a blend of Dravidian and Nagara features, was developed by the Chalukyas for their structural temples.

 

• The Shore Temple belongs to the rival dynasty that humbled the Chalukyas at Vatapi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pattadakal's ten temples show the unique blend of North Indian and South Indian styles.

 

• The Chalukyas of Badami also created the Badami cave temples with fine sculpture and paintings.

 

• The Pallava Shore Temple stands on the Coromandel coast near Chennai.

 

• The Mamallapuram monuments, including the Shore Temple, were listed by UNESCO in 1984 as the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram.

 

NOTE

 

• Aihole Inscription (Option 1): The Aihole Inscription is a Chalukya record composed in the court of Pulakesin II, and so it is firmly linked with the dynasty. It cannot be the unrelated item in this list.

 

• Pattadakal temples (Option 3): Pattadakal lies in Karnataka and its temples, such as the Virupaksha, were made for the Chalukya kings and queens. They form one of the best-known Chalukya monuments.

 

• Vesara style of temples (Option 4): The Vesara style is credited to the Chalukyas of the Deccan, who mixed southern and northern temple forms. It is a typical Chalukya contribution and so it does not answer a NOT question.

question: The Vesara style of temple architecture, developed under the Chalukyas, is a combination of which two styles?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dravidian and Nagara.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Vesara style developed by the Chalukyas for structural temples blends the Dravidian (southern) and Nagara (northern) styles (वेसर शैली — द्रविड़ + नागर)

 

• It is a hybrid style, found especially in the Deccan, and the early experiments took place at Aihole and Pattadakal.

 

• At Pattadakal, some temples follow the Nagara curvilinear tower and others the Dravidian stepped tower, which shows the blending.

 

• The style was developed further by later dynasties such as the Hoysalas of the Deccan.

 

• The Chalukyas thus acted as a bridge between northern and southern temple traditions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three main temple styles are Nagara in the north, Dravidian in the south and Vesara in the Deccan.

 

• Pattadakal was the coronation site of the Chalukya rulers.

 

• Dravidian temples have a vimana and gopuram, while Nagara temples have a shikhara.

 

• The three main Indian temple styles are Nagara, Dravidian and Vesara, and the Hoysala temples at Belur and Halebidu are also called Vesara in style.

 

NOTE

 

• Gandhara and Mathura (Option 1): Gandhara and Mathura were schools of sculpture of the Kushana age and they dealt with Buddhist figure art. They have nothing to do with temple architecture of the Deccan.

 

• Nagara and Indo-Islamic (Option 2): Indo-Islamic architecture arose after the Turkish conquest of north India in the 12th and 13th centuries. It came after the Chalukyas, and Nagara was never blended with it in the Vesara style.

 

• Greek and Dravidian (Option 4): Greek art influenced the Gandhara school in the north-west after Alexander's invasion. There is no Greek element in Chalukya temple building.

question: The finest paintings of the Chalukya period are found in which of the following?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Badami cave temple.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The finest Chalukya paintings are found in the Badami cave temple in Karnataka, a rock-cut shrine of the Chalukya capital Vatapi (बादामी गुफा मंदिर — चालुक्य चित्रकला)

 

• The Badami caves were excavated in the sandstone hills in the time of rulers such as Mangalesha, and include Hindu and Jain shrines.

 

• The paintings show the high skill of Chalukya artists, who worked on the walls and ceilings of the rock-cut caves.

 

• The Chalukya artists thus worked in both sculpture and painting, in addition to architecture.

 

• Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal together make up the main Chalukya sites.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Cave 3 at Badami is dedicated to Vishnu and has an inscription dated 578 AD.

 

• Dakshinachitra, a text on painting, is linked with the Pallava king Mahendravarman I.

 

• The Badami caves lie around a lake called Agastya Tirtha.

 

• Wall paintings of Pallava times are known from the Sittanavasal caves in Tamil Nadu, and those of the Ajanta caves cover many centuries from the Satavahana to the Vakataka age.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahabalipuram rathas (Option 2): The Mahabalipuram rathas are monolithic stone temples carved by the Pallavas, and they are known for sculpture and not for painting. They belong to the Pallava rather than to the Chalukya art.

 

• Elephanta caves (Option 3): Elephanta is an island shrine near Mumbai, known for its large Shiva sculptures in the form of Trimurti. It is famous for stone sculpture and not for Chalukya painting.

 

• Sanchi stupa (Option 4): The Sanchi stupa is a Buddhist monument of the Mauryan and Sunga age in Madhya Pradesh. It has carved gateways and no relation to Chalukya wall-painting.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Rashtrakutas:

1. They were Tamil in origin.

2. Their founder was Tailapa II.

3. They were worshippers of Shiva.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only statement 3 is correct: the Rashtrakutas were followers and worshippers of Shiva; they were Kannada in origin (not Tamil) and their founder was Dantidurga, not Tailapa II (राष्ट्रकूट — कन्नड़ मूल, शैव, संस्थापक दंतिदुर्ग)

 

• Kannada was the mother tongue of the Rashtrakutas, and they patronised Kannada literature.

 

• Tailapa II was a feudatory of the Rashtrakutas who later overthrew them and set up the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.

 

• The Shaiva faith of the dynasty is seen in the great Kailasa temple at Ellora and the Shiva shrines of Elephanta.

 

• The dynasty ruled the Deccan and took part in the Tripartite struggle for Kannauj.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rashtrakuta kings patronised Jainism, Shaivism and Vaishnavism alike.

 

• Kannada literature grew under Amoghavarsha I, to whom the Kavirajamarga is attributed.

 

• Arab travellers called the Rashtrakuta king Balhara.

 

• The Rashtrakuta kingdom stretched over modern Maharashtra and northern Karnataka, with a branch line ruling parts of Gujarat.

 

• Rashtrakuta rulers also fought the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Palas in the north and the Cholas and Pallavas in the south, so the dynasty was a powerful all-India force in its day.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 1): This choice claims a Tamil origin for the dynasty. The Rashtrakutas were of Kannada origin, with Kannada as their mother tongue, so statement 1 is wrong.

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 3): This pair accepts the claim of Tamil origin and also names Tailapa II as the founder. Both are errors, since the dynasty was Kannada and Dantidurga founded it.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 4): This pair includes Tailapa II as the founder, which is wrong, since he destroyed the Rashtrakutas to found the Western Chalukyas. It also leaves out the correct statement about the worship of Shiva.

question: Who built the famous rock-cut Shiva (Kailasa) temple at Ellora?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Krishna I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Krishna I, the uncle of Dantidurga, built the famous Kailasa temple at Ellora, a monolithic rock-cut Shiva temple in the Dravidian style (कैलास मंदिर, एलोरा — कृष्ण प्रथम)

 

• The temple was carved from a single rock by cutting down from the top, and is one of the world's largest monolithic structures.

 

• Its three-tiered sikhara (tower) resembles the sikhara of the Mamallapuram rathas of the Pallavas.

 

• Ellora belongs to Buddhist, Hindu and Jain traditions, with 34 caves in all, mainly made under Rashtrakuta rule.

 

• The Kailasa temple is thus the greatest monument of the Rashtrakuta dynasty.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ellora is a UNESCO World Heritage Site near Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar) in Maharashtra.

 

• The Kailasa temple is Cave 16 of the Ellora group.

 

• The Kailasa temple is believed to have been inspired by the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal.

 

• The Kailasa temple was carved from the top downwards by removing rock from a hillside, and it imitates a free-standing structural temple complex.

 

NOTE

 

• Dantidurga (Option 2): Dantidurga founded the dynasty and overthrew the Chalukya Kirtivarman II, but the Kailasa temple was raised by his successor. He is credited with the foundation of the dynasty and not with this great rock-cut shrine.

 

• Amoghavarsha I (Option 3): Amoghavarsha I ruled for 64 years and built the capital at Manyakheta; he was known for his patronage of literature and Jainism. The Kailasa temple was built a generation earlier.

 

• Govinda III (Option 4): Govinda III was a warrior king who defeated Dharmapala and won in the Tripartite struggle for Kannauj. His fame rests on conquests and not on the building of the Ellora temple.

question: The Hiranyagarbha (Golden womb) ritual, performed by non-Kshatriya rulers such as the Rashtrakuta Dantidurga, was conducted with the help of which group?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Brahmanas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Hiranyagarbha ritual was conducted with the help of Brahmanas, who performed the rites that gave a ruler a ritual rebirth and a Kshatriya status, as in the case of Dantidurga (हिरण्यगर्भ अनुष्ठान — ब्राह्मण पुरोहित)

 

• In the ritual the ruler was symbolically placed in a golden pot (womb) and 'reborn' as a twice-born with a higher social rank.

 

• It was used by non-Kshatriya rulers who needed social acceptance, because the Rashtrakutas were not of the traditional warrior class.

 

• Such rites show the rising power of Brahmanas as priests and the growth of land grants to them in early medieval India.

 

• Brahmanical rituals thus helped new ruling families to legitimise their power.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Another similar ritual was Tulapurusha-dana, in which a king was weighed against gold and gave it away.

 

• Dantidurga is said to have performed the ritual at Ujjain.

 

• Several early medieval dynasties of non-Kshatriya origin sought such rituals.

 

• Early medieval kings also performed rites like Rajasuya, Ashvamedha and Vajapeya, and Brahmana priests got land grants as gifts for such ceremonies.

 

NOTE

 

• Kshatriyas (Option 1): Kshatriyas were the warrior class for whom the ritual was meant to make a non-Kshatriya ruler socially equal. They were the status being acquired and were not the priests who performed the rites.

 

• Vaishyas (Option 3): Vaishyas were the trading and farming class, and had no priestly role in Vedic-style rituals. They could not have conducted a Brahmanical rebirth ritual.

 

• Shudras (Option 4): Shudras were the labouring class and were not permitted to conduct or take part in Vedic rituals of this kind. They were not the performers of the Hiranyagarbha.

question: Krishna I, who succeeded the Rashtrakuta founder Dantidurga, was related to him as his:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uncle.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Krishna I was the uncle of Dantidurga and succeeded him to the Rashtrakuta throne, completing the overthrow of Chalukya power (कृष्ण प्रथम — दंतिदुर्ग के चाचा)

 

• Dantidurga left no son to succeed him, and so the throne passed to his uncle in the collateral line.

 

• Krishna I extended Rashtrakuta power over a large part of the Deccan, including areas once ruled by the Badami Chalukyas.

 

• He is remembered for building the Kailasa temple at Ellora, a rock-cut Shiva temple.

 

• His reign thus marks the consolidation of the dynasty started by his nephew.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Rashtrakutas used the title Prithvivallabha for several kings.

 

• Krishna I's successor was his son Govinda II, followed by Dhruva.

 

• Dhruva was the first Rashtrakuta king to take part in the struggle for Kannauj.

 

• Krishna I took the title Shubhatunga, and under him the Rashtrakutas ended the Chalukya remnants and also fought the Gangas of Karnataka.

 

NOTE

 

• Son (Option 1): Krishna I was not the son of Dantidurga. Dantidurga's own line did not continue on the throne, and the crown went to a relative of the older generation instead.

 

• Younger brother (Option 2): Krishna I was not the younger brother of Dantidurga but belonged to the previous generation as the uncle. This is the clear statement of relationship in the Rashtrakuta record.

 

• Grandson (Option 3): Krishna I was not a grandson, because he succeeded Dantidurga directly. A grandson would belong to a later generation and could not have followed him on the throne.

question: Which Rashtrakuta ruler defeated the Pala king Dharmapala and won the Tripartite war of Kannauj?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Govinda III.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Govinda III defeated the Pala king Dharmapala and was successful in the Tripartite struggle for Kannauj, which made the Rashtrakutas the leading power of the age (गोविंद तृतीय — धर्मपाल को पराजित किया)

 

• The Tripartite struggle was fought between the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Palas and the Rashtrakutas for Kannauj in the 8th-10th centuries.

 

• Govinda III's campaigns carried Rashtrakuta arms to the north, as far as the Himalayan foothills according to the records.

 

• Despite his victory, no dynasty gained permanent supremacy in the north, and the Rashtrakutas returned to the Deccan.

 

• His success raised the prestige of the dynasty and prepared its golden age under Amoghavarsha I.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dharmapala was the second ruler of the Pala dynasty of Bengal and Bihar and a patron of Vikramashila.

 

• Kannauj was prized because of its position, prestige and its control of the Gangetic plains.

 

• The Pala and Pratihara kings had also fought each other for Kannauj.

 

• Govinda III's reign saw wars against the Pallavas, Gangas and Vengi Chalukyas as well, and he also installed his brother Indra as ruler of Gujarat.

 

NOTE

 

• Dantidurga (Option 1): Dantidurga founded the dynasty in the mid-8th century and was not involved in the Kannauj wars against Dharmapala. His rule belonged to the age before the struggle took shape.

 

• Krishna I (Option 2): Krishna I was the builder of the Kailasa temple and a consolidator of Rashtrakuta power in the Deccan. His reign was too early for the Pala king Dharmapala to be his opponent in Kannauj.

 

• Krishna III (Option 4): Krishna III ruled in the 10th century and is famous for his southern campaign against the Cholas at Takkolam. He lived long after Dharmapala, so he could not have defeated him.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha I:

1. He ruled for 64 years.

2. He was the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty.

3. He built the Rashtrakuta capital at Malkhed (Manyakheta).

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Truth lies with 1 and 3: Amoghavarsha I (815-880 AD) ruled for 64 years and built the capital at Malkhed (Manyakheta); statement 2 is false because the dynasty was founded by Dantidurga (अमोघवर्ष प्रथम — मान्यखेट, 64 वर्ष शासन)

 

• His long reign was among the longest in Indian history, and it was a time of cultural growth for the Rashtrakutas.

 

• He was a patron of Kannada literature and is traditionally credited with the Kavirajamarga, the earliest available work on Kannada poetics.

 

• He was a follower of Jainism in his later life, and his teacher was the Jain monk Jinasena.

 

• Manyakheta remained the Rashtrakuta capital for the rest of the dynasty's rule.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Arab traveller Sulaiman called the Rashtrakuta king (Balhara) one of the four great kings of the world.

 

• Amoghavarsha's reign was troubled by revolts of feudatories, but he held the empire together.

 

• Kavirajamarga shows the status of Kannada as a literary language in the 9th century.

 

• Amoghavarsha I is also credited with a Sanskrit work of moral questions and answers, the Prashnottara Ratnamalika, which is a Jain text.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 1): Taking only statement 1 overlooks the fact that he built Manyakheta as the capital, which makes statement 3 correct too. So this choice is incomplete.

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 2): Statement 2 is the problem in this pair. Dantidurga, who overthrew Kirtivarman II, was the dynasty's founder, and Amoghavarsha I was a much later ruler.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): Here statement 2 is again accepted, and it is wrong since Amoghavarsha was not the founder. This pair also leaves out the true statement 1 on his 64-year reign.

question: Which Rashtrakuta king defeated the Chola ruler Parantaka I at Takkolam?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Krishna III.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Krishna III (936-968 AD) defeated the Cholas under Parantaka I at Takkolam and set up pillars of victory at Rameshwaram (कृष्ण तृतीय — तक्कोलम की लड़ाई, चोलों पर विजय)

 

• He was famous for his southern expeditions and for establishing Rashtrakuta power in the Tamil country for a time.

 

• The victory at Takkolam checked the rise of the Cholas and delayed their expansion until the Rashtrakuta decline.

 

• The notes record that he built Pillars of Victory in a temple at Rameshwaram, on the southern tip of India.

 

• He was among the last great Rashtrakuta kings, since the dynasty fell soon after his death.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Chola prince Rajaditya, son of Parantaka I, was killed in the battle of Takkolam in about 949 AD.

 

• The Cholas recovered under Rajaraja I a few decades later.

 

• Rashtrakuta power ended in the 970s when Tailapa II overthrew the dynasty.

 

• The Chola recovery after Takkolam came only under Rajaraja I, who built the strong Chola empire and raised the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur.

 

NOTE

 

• Krishna I (Option 2): Krishna I ruled in the 8th century and consolidated Rashtrakuta rule in the Deccan, besides building the Kailasa temple. He lived more than a century and a half before Parantaka I and could not have fought him.

 

• Dantidurga (Option 3): Dantidurga founded the dynasty in the 8th century, long before the Chola ruler Parantaka I came to the throne. The two could never have met in battle.

 

• Govinda III (Option 4): Govinda III belonged to the early 9th century and fought the Palas and Pratiharas in the north. Parantaka I ruled in the early 10th century, so Govinda III cannot be the victor at Takkolam.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Rashtrakuta king Krishna III:

1. He defeated the Cholas under Parantaka I at Takkolam.

2. He set up Pillars of Victory in a temple at Rameshwaram.

3. He built the Kailasa temple at Ellora.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 1 and 2 are accurate: Krishna III beat the Cholas at Takkolam and set up Pillars of Victory at Rameshwaram; statement 3 is wrong since the Kailasa temple was built by Krishna I (कृष्ण तृतीय — रामेश्वरम में विजय स्तंभ)

 

• Krishna III's campaigns were the farthest southern thrust of the Rashtrakutas and reached the tip of the peninsula.

 

• Krishna I and Krishna III were separated by about a century and a half, so it is easy to mix up their works.

 

• The Kailasa temple at Ellora is a rock-cut monolithic Dravidian-style temple, which belongs to the early phase of the dynasty.

 

• After Krishna III, the Rashtrakuta kingdom weakened rapidly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rameshwaram is on an island in Tamil Nadu and has one of the twelve Jyotirlingas.

 

• Krishna III's rule is dated 936-968 AD in the notes.

 

• Tailapa II, a feudatory, overthrew the weakened Rashtrakutas after his death.

 

• Krishna III also took Kanchi and Tanjore for a time, and an inscription records the capture of the Chola capital by his army.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 1): Taking only statement 1 misses the pillars of victory at Rameshwaram, which is a well-recorded achievement of Krishna III. So statement 2 is also true.

 

• Only 3 (Option 2): Statement 3 alone is false, because Krishna I built the Kailasa temple at Ellora. It also fails to mention the victories at Takkolam and Rameshwaram that mark Krishna III's reign.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Accepting all three is wrong because of statement 3, which attributes the Ellora temple to the wrong king. The Kailasa temple belongs to Krishna I, long before Krishna III.

question: The Elephanta caves near Mumbai are dedicated to which deity, shown in the form of Trimurti?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shiva.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Elephanta caves, on an island near Mumbai, were dedicated to Shiva, whose Trimurti form is the great masterpiece of the shrine (एलीफेंटा गुफाएँ — शिव की त्रिमूर्ति)

 

• The central sculpture shows a three-headed figure of Shiva as creator, preserver and destroyer, and it is a huge relief in the main hall.

 

• The cave site also has other sculptures of Shiva, such as Ardhanarishvara, Nataraja and the marriage of Shiva and Parvati.

 

• Along with Ellora, Elephanta is one of the great rock-cut sites of the Deccan, and the notes group it with Rashtrakuta art.

 

• Elephanta is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The island is also known as Gharapuri and lies in Mumbai harbour.

 

• The Portuguese gave the island the name Elephanta after a large stone elephant statue that stood there.

 

• The Elephanta caves include Hindu and a few Buddhist excavations.

 

• The great Maheshamurti sculpture at Elephanta is more than five metres high, and the island lies nearly 10 km from the Gateway of India.

 

NOTE

 

• Vishnu (Option 1): Vishnu is the preserver in the Trimurti and has a separate cult, but the Elephanta caves are best known for the Shiva sculptures. The famous image shows Shiva and not Vishnu.

 

• Buddha (Option 2): The Buddha is the central figure of the Buddhist caves of Ajanta and Karle, and there is no Trimurti form of the Buddha. The Elephanta sculptures are Shaiva.

 

• Surya (Option 4): Surya is the sun-god, who has famous temples at Konark and Modhera. The main sculpture at Elephanta is not a Surya image.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Ellora caves:

1. They include Buddhist caves.

2. They include Hindu caves.

3. They include Jain caves.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All three statements are correct: the Ellora caves (34 caves) belong to Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism, and were built mainly under the Rashtrakutas, with the great Kailasa temple built by Krishna I (एलोरा गुफाएँ — बौद्ध, हिंदू, जैन)

 

• Ellora has about 12 Buddhist, 17 Hindu and 5 Jain caves, which were made over a long period.

 

• This mixture shows the religious tolerance of the Deccan kingdoms of that time.

 

• The Hindu group includes the monolithic Kailasa temple, the greatest of its caves.

 

• Ellora is in Maharashtra, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Buddhist caves of Ellora are the oldest, followed by the Hindu and Jain caves.

 

• Cave 10 at Ellora is a Buddhist chaitya hall called Vishvakarma cave.

 

• The Jain caves, such as the Indra Sabha, were made in the last phase.

 

• Ellora's Cave 16, the Kailasa temple, is a Hindu monument, whereas the Buddhist caves 1-12 are of the earlier period of the 5th to 7th centuries.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Only two of the three religions are named in this choice, but the Jain caves at Ellora are also real. The group of caves is truly mixed in religion.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): This choice leaves out the Buddhist caves, which are actually the earliest group at Ellora, and are well known for the Vishvakarma chaitya hall.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): This choice leaves out the Hindu caves, which include the Kailasa temple, the best-known monument of the site. The omission makes it wrong.

question: Which of the following three powers fought the Tripartite Struggle for control over Kannauj during the early medieval period?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas and Palas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj was fought among the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Rashtrakutas and the Palas during the 8th-10th centuries CE (त्रिपक्षीय संघर्ष — प्रतिहार, राष्ट्रकूट, पाल)

 

• The Pratiharas held western and northern India, the Palas ruled Bengal and Bihar, and the Rashtrakutas ruled the Deccan.

 

• Kannauj was important for its location, political prestige and control of the rich Gangetic plains.

 

• In the end, no dynasty achieved lasting supremacy, and the long conflict weakened all three powers.

 

• This political fragmentation later made North India more open to Turkish invasions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Rashtrakuta kings who took part in the conflict include Dhruva, Govinda III and Indra III.

 

• The Pala king Dharmapala and the Pratihara Nagabhata II also fought for Kannauj.

 

• The rulers of Kannauj for a time were the Ayudha kings, who were a prize of the struggle.

 

• Nagabhata II of the Gurjara-Pratiharas was defeated by Govinda III, but the Pratiharas later made Kannauj their capital.

 

NOTE

 

• Pallavas, Chalukyas and Satavahanas (Option 1): The Pallavas and Chalukyas were rivals in the south, and the Satavahanas had ended centuries earlier. None of them fought over Kannauj in the 8th-10th centuries.

 

• Paramaras, Chauhans and Chandellas (Option 2): The Paramaras, Chauhans and Chandellas were Rajput houses of the 10th-12th centuries in central and western India. They came later and were not the three contestants for Kannauj.

 

• Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas (Option 4): The Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas were the Tamil kingdoms of the far south, with no involvement in the northern struggle. They fought for supremacy in their own region.

question:
Match the following powers of the Tripartite Struggle with their regions or aims:

a. Gurjara-Pratiharas

b. Palas

c. Rashtrakutas

d. Main object of the struggle

i. Deccan

ii. Kannauj

iii. Western and Northern India

iv. Bengal and Bihar
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii: Gurjara-Pratiharas held Western and Northern India, the Palas held Bengal and Bihar, the Rashtrakutas held the Deccan, and the prize was Kannauj (त्रिपक्षीय संघर्ष — क्षेत्र और उद्देश्य)

 

• The struggle lasted for about two centuries and was a contest for the rich Ganga valley and for imperial prestige.

 

• Kannauj was the former capital of Harsha and carried the status of being the seat of the paramount ruler of North India.

 

• The result was that no dynasty gained permanent supremacy.

 

• All three powers were weakened by the prolonged fighting.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pala kingdom's heartland lay in Bengal and Bihar, with Pataliputra and Gauda as important centres.

 

• The Pratiharas were also called Gurjara-Pratiharas, and they later made Kannauj their capital.

 

• The Rashtrakutas sent armies north repeatedly but could not rule there permanently.

 

• The Pala emperor Dharmapala and the Pratihara king Nagabhata II both contested Kannauj, and the Pala ruler first placed Chakrayudha on the throne there.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii (Option 1): This arrangement swaps the regions of the Pratiharas and the Palas. The Palas ruled in the east, in Bengal and Bihar, while the Pratiharas dominated the west and north, so the first two pairs are wrong.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii (Option 3): This arrangement gives Bengal and Bihar to the Rashtrakutas and the Deccan to the Palas. The Rashtrakutas were a Deccan power and the Palas an eastern power, so those pairs are mixed up.

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-iii, d-ii (Option 4): Here the Pratiharas are placed in the Deccan and the Rashtrakutas in Western India. The Rashtrakutas ruled the Deccan from Karnataka and Maharashtra, so the first and third pairs are exchanged.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Tripartite Struggle:

1. The Rashtrakutas achieved permanent supremacy over North India.

2. The prolonged conflict weakened the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas.

3. The resulting political fragmentation made North India more vulnerable to Turkish invasions.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• On checking each claim, 2 and 3 are correct: the long Tripartite Struggle weakened the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas and left North India divided and open to Turkish invasions; statement 1 is false because no one gained permanent supremacy (त्रिपक्षीय संघर्ष का परिणाम — तुर्क आक्रमण की भूमिका)

 

• The Rashtrakutas won several victories, such as the ones by Dhruva and Govinda III, but they always returned to the Deccan.

 

• The three powers wasted their men and resources in a long war over one city, Kannauj, and left no strong power to guard the north-west.

 

• When the Ghaznavids and later the Ghurids came from the north-west, the divided Rajput states could not form a united front.

 

• The struggle shows how a contest for prestige led to long-term political weakness.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahmud of Ghazni sacked Kannauj in 1018 AD, during the reign of the Pratihara ruler Rajyapala.

 

• The Pratihara empire declined after the raid of the Rashtrakuta king Indra III on Kannauj around 916 AD.

 

• The Palas lost power in the north after Dharmapala and Devapala.

 

• After the Tripartite Struggle, Mahmud of Ghazni attacked northern India from 1000 AD, and Muhammad of Ghor later defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in 1192 AD.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 1): Statement 1 alone is wrong, since the Rashtrakutas never made Kannauj a permanent part of their kingdom. This answer also ignores the two correct statements on the weakening of the powers.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): This pair accepts the claim of permanent Rashtrakuta supremacy, which is false because they went back to the Deccan after each campaign. It also leaves out the correct statement 2.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Accepting all three statements includes the claim of permanent Rashtrakuta supremacy, which is false. The actual result of the struggle was that no dynasty held North India for long.

question:
Assertion (A): Kannauj was the main object of the Tripartite Struggle.

Reason (R): Kannauj was strategically important because of its location, political prestige and control over the rich Gangetic plains.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and R explains A: Kannauj was fought over by the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas because its location, prestige and hold over the Gangetic plains made it valuable (कन्नौज — त्रिपक्षीय संघर्ष का केंद्र)

 

• The city had been the capital of Harsha, and its possession gave the ruler a claim to be the paramount power in the north.

 

• Control of Kannauj also meant access to the rich revenue of the Ganga-Yamuna doab.

 

• The struggle ran for around two centuries, from the 8th to the 10th century.

 

• In the end, none of the three powers held the city permanently, and all three were drained of strength.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kannauj later became the Pratihara capital under Mihira Bhoja.

 

• The Gahadavalas later ruled Kannauj in the 11th-12th centuries.

 

• Kannauj's trade routes connected the Punjab with the lower Ganga valley.

 

• Kannauj finally passed to the Ghurids in 1194 AD, after the Gahadavala king Jayachandra was defeated at Chandawar by Muhammad of Ghor.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This choice says R fails to explain A, but the reasons stated in R are exactly why the powers fought for Kannauj. R is therefore the direct explanation and not a loose fact.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): This choice treats R as false. The location, prestige and access to the Gangetic plains are the recorded reasons for the importance of Kannauj, so R is a sound statement.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): This choice makes A false, but Kannauj was indeed the central prize of the Tripartite Struggle between the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas.

question:
Match the following Rashtrakuta kings with their achievements:

a. Dantidurga

b. Krishna I

c. Govinda III

d. Amoghavarsha I

i. Defeated the Pala king Dharmapala

ii. Founded the dynasty by overthrowing Kirtivarman II

iii. Built the capital at Manyakheta

iv. Built the Kailasa temple at Ellora
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct matching is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii: Dantidurga founded the dynasty, Krishna I built the Kailasa temple, Govinda III defeated Dharmapala, and Amoghavarsha I built Manyakheta (राष्ट्रकूट शासक — दंतिदुर्ग, कृष्ण प्रथम, गोविंद तृतीय, अमोघवर्ष)

 

• The sequence of the four kings follows the order of the dynasty's rise, from founder to the peak of its power.

 

• Dantidurga is also believed to have been a feudatory of the Chalukyas before his revolt.

 

• Amoghavarsha I ruled for 64 years and was a patron of Kannada literature.

 

• Govinda III won the Tripartite war of Kannauj, which marked the height of Rashtrakuta military power.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Krishna I was the uncle of Dantidurga.

 

• Manyakheta is the modern Malkhed in Karnataka.

 

• The Kailasa temple at Ellora is a monolithic rock-cut shrine in the Dravidian style.

 

• Manyakheta, the Rashtrakuta capital, is the present village of Malkhed in Kalaburagi district of Karnataka.

 

• Dantidurga and Krishna I laid the foundation of Rashtrakuta power, Govinda III raised it to its height, and Amoghavarsha I held it together in a long and peaceful reign.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii (Option 1): This arrangement gives the foundation of the dynasty to Krishna I and the Kailasa temple to Dantidurga. Dantidurga was the founder, and Krishna I built the temple, so the first two links are exchanged.

 

• a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i (Option 2): Here Govinda III is given the capital Manyakheta and Amoghavarsha I the defeat of Dharmapala. The capital was built by Amoghavarsha I, while the Pala king was beaten by Govinda III, so the last two pairs are crossed.

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-ii, d-iii (Option 3): In this arrangement Dantidurga is credited with defeating Dharmapala and Govinda III with the founding of the dynasty. The founder was Dantidurga, and the victor over Dharmapala was Govinda III, so these pairs are wrong.

question:
Arrange the following Pallava rulers in chronological order:

1. Simhavishnu

2. Narasimhavarman I

3. Narasimhavarman II

4. Mahendravarman I
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 4, 2, 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct order is 1, 4, 2, 3: Simhavishnu (c. 575-600), Mahendravarman I (600-630), Narasimhavarman I (630-668) and Narasimhavarman II (695-722) (पल्लव शासकों का क्रम — सिंहविष्णु से राजसिंह तक)

 

• Simhavishnu, the founder, was the father of Mahendravarman I, who was in turn the father of Narasimhavarman I.

 

• Narasimhavarman I avenged the defeat suffered by his father at the hands of Pulakesin II.

 

• Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) ruled after a gap of some years and is known for structural temples.

 

• The architectural sequence follows the same order, from rock-cut caves to monolithic rathas and then structural temples.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Paramesvaravarman I came between Narasimhavarman I and Narasimhavarman II.

 

• Nandivarman II Pallavamalla ruled after Rajasimha's dynasty line was disturbed.

 

• Rajasimha's son Mahendravarman III completed the Kailasanatha temple.

 

• Nandivarman II Pallavamalla came to the throne from a collateral branch of the Pallava family after the direct line of Rajasimha ended.

 

• The usual mnemonic runs from the founder Simhavishnu to his son Mahendravarman I, then to Narasimhavarman I, and later to Rajasimha, who was the builder of the Shore Temple.

 

NOTE

 

• 1, 2, 4, 3 (Option 1): This order puts Narasimhavarman I before Mahendravarman I. The father Mahendravarman I came first and the son Narasimhavarman I second, so the order of the middle two is reversed.

 

• 4, 1, 2, 3 (Option 3): This order starts with Mahendravarman I and puts the founder second. The founder Simhavishnu was the father of Mahendravarman I, so he must come first.

 

• 1, 4, 3, 2 (Option 4): This order puts Narasimhavarman II before Narasimhavarman I. Rajasimha ruled at the end of the 7th century, long after the conqueror of Vatapi, so the last two are interchanged.

question:
Assertion (A): Vikramaditya I of the Chalukyas attacked and defeated the Pallava ruler Paramesvaravarman I.

Reason (R): Vikramaditya I wanted to avenge the defeat of his father Pulakesin II at the hands of the Pallavas.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: A is false but R is true
option_4: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are true and R explains A: Vikramaditya I defeated Paramesvaravarman I to avenge the defeat of Pulakesin II by the Pallavas, which had cost the Chalukyas their capital (विक्रमादित्य प्रथम — पुलकेशिन की हार का बदला)

 

• Pulakesin II had been defeated by Narasimhavarman I, who captured Vatapi and took the title Vatapikonda.

 

• Paramesvaravarman I was the successor of Narasimhavarman I, and so the Chalukya king struck at the successor of his father's conqueror.

 

• The recovery of Chalukya fortunes by Vikramaditya I shows the see-saw pattern of the Pallava-Chalukya rivalry.

 

• The wars of the two dynasties lasted for more than a century and affected art as well as politics.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vikramaditya II later entered Kanchi but spared its temples.

 

• The war also had a cultural effect, as seen in the Pattadakal temples modelled on Kanchi.

 

• The Pallava-Chalukya struggle was a chief theme of South Indian history from the 7th to the 8th century.

 

• Paramesvaravarman I is said to have defeated Vikramaditya I at Peruvalanallur, according to Pallava records, while Chalukya records claim victory for their king.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): This choice says R does not explain A, but the wish for revenge is the very reason given for the attack on the Pallava ruler. R therefore directly explains A.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): This choice accepts A but treats R as false, whereas the defeat of Pulakesin II by the Pallavas is a well-known fact and the reason for the war of revenge.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 3): This choice makes A false, but Vikramaditya I did defeat Paramesvaravarman I and so recovered the Chalukya position after the Pallava triumph.

question:
Consider the following statements about Pallava architecture:

1. The Pallavas introduced the art of cutting temples out of rock in South India.

2. The five rathas of Mahabalipuram were built by Rajasimha.

3. The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram is a structural temple.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The accurate set is 1 and 3: the Pallavas introduced rock-cut temples and the Shore Temple is a structural temple; statement 2 is wrong because the five rathas were carved in the time of Narasimhavarman I (पल्लव स्थापत्य — शैलकृत, एकाश्मक रथ, संरचनात्मक मंदिर)

 

• Rajasimha (Narasimhavarman II) built the Shore Temple and began the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi, both of them structural.

 

• The five rathas are monolithic, cut from single rocks, and were carved earlier in the reign of Narasimhavarman I.

 

• The Pallava sequence thus moved from caves to monolithic rathas and then to structural temples.

 

• These Pallava forms started the Dravidian style.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The rathas are named after the Pandavas and Draupadi, but they are not connected with the epic in worship.

 

• Structural temples are built of cut stone blocks laid in layers, unlike rock-cut shrines.

 

• The Pallava structural temples were the models for Chola temples.

 

• Pallava temple sculpture includes the Durga fighting Mahishasura panel at Mamallapuram, which is a fine example of dynamic rock-cut relief.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 (Option 2): Taking only statement 1 overlooks the Shore Temple, which is a real structural temple built by Rajasimha. So statement 3 is correct as well, and this answer is too short.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 3): This pair takes statement 2 as true, which is a mistake because the rathas belong to the earlier Narasimhavarman I. It also leaves out the correct statement 1 on rock-cut temples.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Marking all three as true accepts the wrong claim that the rathas were built by Rajasimha. They were carved a generation or two earlier under Narasimhavarman I.

question: Which of the following is NOT associated with the Rashtrakutas?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aihole Inscription.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Aihole Inscription was composed by Ravikirti in praise of the Chalukya king Pulakesin II, so it is not connected with the Rashtrakutas; the other three are Rashtrakuta (ऐहोल अभिलेख — चालुक्य, राष्ट्रकूट नहीं)

 

• The Kailasa temple at Ellora is the greatest Rashtrakuta monument and was built by Krishna I.

 

• Manyakheta (Malkhed) was the capital built by Amoghavarsha I.

 

• The victory over Parantaka I at Takkolam was won by Krishna III.

 

• The Aihole record belongs to the earlier dynasty that the Rashtrakutas replaced.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dantidurga overthrew the last Chalukya of Badami, Kirtivarman II, and so replaced the Aihole dynasty.

 

• Aihole is in Karnataka, and its record was composed in the 7th century.

 

• The Rashtrakutas ruled the Deccan for about two centuries.

 

• The Rashtrakuta chief Dhruva was the first of the dynasty to enter the Kannauj contest, and Indra III later sacked Kannauj in the early 10th century.

 

NOTE

 

• Kailasa temple at Ellora (Option 1): The Kailasa temple at Ellora is the finest monument of the Rashtrakutas, built under Krishna I. Because it is a Rashtrakuta work, it cannot be the odd one out here.

 

• Manyakheta (Malkhed) (Option 2): Manyakheta, also called Malkhed, was developed as the Rashtrakuta capital by Amoghavarsha I. It is truly a Rashtrakuta place and is not the answer to a NOT question.

 

• Takkolam victory over the Cholas (Option 4): The battle of Takkolam was a Rashtrakuta victory under Krishna III against the Chola army of Parantaka I. It is associated with the dynasty and so is not the odd item.

question: The Pattadakal group of temples, a UNESCO World Heritage Site famed for blending Northern and Southern styles, is located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Karnataka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pattadakal, with its group of about ten temples built by the Chalukyas, is in Karnataka; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and shows a blend of Nagara and Dravidian styles (पट्टदकल — कर्नाटक, यूनेस्को विश्व धरोहर)

 

• Pattadakal was the place where the Chalukya kings of Badami were crowned.

 

• Its best-known temples are the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples, built by the queens of Vikramaditya II.

 

• The style of the site, called Vesara in later literature, is typical of the Chalukya dynasty.

 

• Together with Aihole and Badami, it lies in the Malaprabha valley of north Karnataka.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pattadakal complex was listed by UNESCO in 1987.

 

• The Papanatha temple at Pattadakal shows Nagara features, while Virupaksha is Dravidian.

 

• The Jain temple at Pattadakal was built under the Rashtrakutas.

 

• The ten Pattadakal temples were built between the late 7th and the 8th centuries, and the Sangameshvara temple there was built by Vijayaditya Satyashraya.

 

NOTE

 

• Tamil Nadu (Option 1): Tamil Nadu has the Pallava monuments of Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram. They are in the Dravidian style of the Pallavas, and Pattadakal lies further north in the Chalukya heartland.

 

• Andhra Pradesh (Option 2): Andhra Pradesh was the home of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, whose capital was in the Godavari-Krishna delta. The Pattadakal group belongs to the Badami Chalukyas in Karnataka.

 

• Maharashtra (Option 3): Maharashtra has Ellora and Elephanta, which are Rashtrakuta-era rock-cut sites. Pattadakal is a Chalukya site and is not in this state.

question: After the fall of their independent kingdom, the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi continued up to about 1189 CE as feudatories of which dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cholas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi ruled until about 1130 CE and then carried on as feudatories of the Cholas until about 1189 CE (वेंगी के पूर्वी चालुक्य — चोलों के सामंत)

 

• Their kingdom lay in present-day Andhra Pradesh, between the Godavari and the Krishna.

 

• Chola ties with the Vengi house were strengthened by marriage alliances, and a later Chola ruler descended from this line.

 

• The Eastern Chalukyas had arisen from the viceroyalty of Vishnuvardhana after the death of Pulakesin II.

 

• Vengi's long contest with the Cholas and the Western Chalukyas shaped the politics of the Deccan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kulottunga I was the son of an Eastern Chalukya prince and a Chola princess.

 

• Vengi was a fertile and rich region, which made it a prize for rival powers.

 

• Telugu literature began to develop under the Eastern Chalukya patronage.

 

• The Chola ruler Rajaraja I restored the Eastern Chalukya prince Saktivarman I to the throne of Vengi, which shows the Chola grip on this region.

 

NOTE

 

• Pandyas (Option 1): The Pandyas ruled the far south of Tamil Nadu and were rivals of the Cholas. The Eastern Chalukya state was in Andhra, and the Pandyas did not take it as their vassal.

 

• Hoysalas (Option 2): The Hoysalas were a Karnataka dynasty of the later period, whose power was in Dwarasamudra. They did not control Vengi in coastal Andhra.

 

• Rashtrakutas (Option 4): The Rashtrakutas had fallen in the 10th century, long before the later phase of the Eastern Chalukyas. They could not have been the overlords in the 12th century.

question: Before founding the Rashtrakuta dynasty, Dantidurga is believed to have been a feudatory of which dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chalukyas of Badami.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dantidurga is believed to have been a feudatory of the Chalukyas of Badami before he overthrew Kirtivarman II and founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty (दंतिदुर्ग — बादामी चालुक्यों का सामंत)

 

• His success was an example of a feudatory growing strong and replacing his own overlord, a pattern of early medieval India.

 

• The overthrow of Kirtivarman II ended the Badami Chalukya dynasty after about two centuries.

 

• The same pattern was repeated when Tailapa II, a feudatory of the Rashtrakutas, overthrew them and founded the Western Chalukyas.

 

• The Rashtrakutas were of Kannada origin and followers of Shiva.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Hiranyagarbha ritual helped Dantidurga to claim a higher status.

 

• The word Rashtrakuta comes from rashtrakuta, meaning a provincial officer or chief.

 

• Feudatories (samantas) were important in the politics of early medieval India.

 

• Dantidurga bore titles such as Prithvivallabha and Khadgavaloka in his records, which marked his claim to be a sovereign ruler.

 

NOTE

 

• Pallavas of Kanchi (Option 2): The Pallavas of Kanchi were the long-time rivals of the Chalukyas and ruled in the Tamil plains. Dantidurga was a Deccan chief and was not their vassal.

 

• Gurjara-Pratiharas (Option 3): The Gurjara-Pratiharas ruled in western and northern India and later fought Dantidurga's successors for Kannauj. They were rivals of the Rashtrakutas and not their overlords.

 

• Palas of Bengal (Option 4): The Palas of Bengal and Bihar were the eastern powers who also fought for Kannauj. They had no authority over the Deccan, so they could not have been Dantidurga's overlords.
